claims.text: Combined wear-corrosion resistance in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and maintenance of a nanostructured, self-healing oxide film.
Segregation and surface enrichment of passivating elements such as Cr and Al produce the protective oxide film.
Enrichment in Cr or Al promotes rapid re-establishment of the protective barrier after mechanical removal.
The relevant surface film is nanostructured, adherent, and enriched in passivating elements.
The enriched oxide film is mechanically stable and self-healing under simultaneous abrasion and chloride exposure.
Preferential segregation of passivating elements during combined mechanical and corrosive loading leads to rapid protective-oxide formation.
An adherent and regenerable oxide minimizes synergistic wear-corrosion damage by rapidly repassivating freshly exposed metal.
An alloy with optimized oxide-former content will have a lower combined material-loss rate than a matched alloy with reduced oxide-former content.
The optimized alloy will have lower wear-related material loss than the matched baseline.
The optimized alloy will have lower corrosion-related material loss than the matched baseline.
Reducing the concentration of critical oxide-forming elements results in a less protective or more slowly regenerating oxide film.
The predicted advantage should hold at moderate temperature, controlled abrasive stress, and moderate chloride aggressiveness.
Much higher temperatures, more aggressive chemical environments, or extremely high mechanical loads can prevent formation or maintenance of the protective film and diminish the resistance advantage.
A controlled comparison can test the hypothesis by exposing oxide-former-rich and oxide-former-reduced alloy variants to identical reciprocating sliding conditions in 3.5 wt% NaCl at 60°C.
Similar combined degradation rates together with no significant difference in oxide formation, adherence, or regeneration would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
